query: Consider the following context: Materials capable of withstanding extreme environments open promising opportunities for nuclear fusion reactors. In that context, which material can be used for interlayer materials between W and CuCrZr, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A quinary refractory high‐entropy alloy (HEA) – for example one based on W, Ta, Cr, V, and Hf – can serve as an effective interlayer between tungsten (W) and CuCrZr in fusion reactor components.
generation.material_initial_state: W and CuCrZr components with their inherent large differences in thermal expansion and irradiation response, which normally lead to interface stress and degradation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a thin film or coating of a quinary refractory HEA (e.g., W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf) as an interlayer between the tungsten and CuCrZr layers.
generation.conditions: Service conditions relevant to nuclear fusion reactors including extreme thermal loads, high neutron irradiation, and rapid thermal cycling.
generation.structural_mediator: The HEA interlayer forming a graded or compatible bonding zone exhibits nanocrystalline or fine-grained refractory microstructure that bridges the lattice and thermal expansion differences between W and CuCrZr.
generation.mechanism: Owing to its high thermal stability and excellent resistance to irradiation damage, the HEA interlayer mediates the stress arising from mismatched coefficients of thermal expansion. Its refractory nature and solid-solution strengthening help limit interdiffusion and phase degradation at the interface, thereby reducing crack initiation and propagation under severe operating conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The introduction of the HEA interlayer is predicted to improve bonding between W and CuCrZr, reduce thermal stress and interfacial degradation, and enhance overall durability under fusion reactor conditions.
generation.baseline: Without an interlayer, the significant mismatch in thermal and irradiation properties between tungsten and CuCrZr leads to high interfacial stresses, rapid degradation due to interdiffusion, and premature failure in extreme environments.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under reactor-relevant thermal and irradiation environments; uncertainties remain on the long-term stability and quantitative performance improvements, which need extended experimental validation.
generation.uncertainty: While refractory HEAs show promising properties in separate studies, the precise interfacial behavior and long-term performance of a W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf interlayer in an actual fusion reactor component are not yet fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of joint samples: one with a thin HEA (W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf) interlayer between tungsten and CuCrZr, and one without an interlayer. Subject both sets to repeated thermal cycles and neutron irradiation that mimic fusion reactor conditions.
measurements: Interfacial microstructure analysis (SEM/TEM) to check for crack or phase formation
Mechanical tests (shear strength, fracture toughness) at room and elevated temperatures
Thermal cycling tests to assess stress-induced delamination
Irradiation damage evaluation via post-irradiation examination
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA interlayer does not show a statistically significant improvement in interfacial integrity (i.e. reduced crack formation, higher mechanical strength, and better resistance to irradiation-induced degradation) compared to joints without the interlayer, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations
